Empirical Research Plan  
“Tariffs, Imported Inputs, and Firm-Level Productivity: Evidence from Indonesian Manufacturing, 1991-2001”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences with continuous treatment intensity, implemented as a triple-difference where necessary.

Rationale  
•  Substantial within-industry, over-time variation in both output and input tariffs generated by exogenous WTO-driven liberalisation.  
•  All firms are observed before and after the major liberalisation wave (pre-1995 vs. post-1995), but the size of the tariff cut differs sharply across 5-digit ISIC industries → “quasi-experiment” suitable for DID.  
•  The research question also asks whether effects differ for firms that import intermediates.  A DDD specification (time × industry-specific tariff change × importer status) cleanly captures that heterogeneity while differencing out common shocks.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variables  
  •  InputTariff_it : Ad-valorem tariff (%) on intermediate inputs faced by industry i in year t (cost-share weighted using 1998 input mix).  
  •  OutputTariff_it : Ad-valorem tariff (%) on final goods in industry i in year t.

Key “treatments”  
  – Large reductions in InputTariff_it (cost shifters).  
  – Large reductions in OutputTariff_it (competition shifters).

Control groups / Counterfactuals  
  •  Industries with small or zero tariff cuts serve as controls for industries with large cuts (standard DID).  
  •  Within an industry, non-importing plants proxy for what would have happened to importing plants had input tariffs not been cut (DDD).

Timing  
  •  Pre-period: 1991–1994 (before WTO accession).  
  •  Post-period: 1995–2001, with year-by-year variation exploited in panel regressions.

No RDD is involved; no single cutoff exists.

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent tariff cuts, productivity in high-cut and low-cut industries would have followed similar trajectories, and importing and non-importing firms within an industry would have evolved similarly.

Plausibility: Pre-1995 tariff levels were driven by a long-standing escalated structure rather than recent industry performance; Indonesia lacks evidence of politically-motivated tariff setting.  We will test this assumption with pre-trend event-study graphs and placebo regressions (see Sec. 5).

A2. Exogeneity of tariff changes: Industry-year tariff schedules were set by multi-lateral commitments, not by contemporaneous industry shocks.

Plausibility: WTO binding schedule, ceiling bindings to ≤40 %, and the fact that the biggest cuts occurred where initial tariffs were highest support exogeneity.

A3. Stable importer status (for DDD): A plant’s baseline (pre-1995) importer status is uncorrelated with post-1995 productivity shocks except through input tariffs.

Plausibility: 1991–1994 importer status reflects technology and supplier networks that are slow to change; we will define “importer” using the 1991-1994 average to minimise endogeneity.

A4. No spillovers between treated and control units: Productivity effects in one industry do not mechanically change tariffs in others.

Plausibility: Indonesian tariffs are set at the national level and not revised based on short-run productivity outcomes.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
-------------------------------------------------
T1. Mean reversion / differential pre-trends  
   – Test: event-study coefficients for 1991–1994 should be flat.  
   – Mitigation: include industry-specific linear pre-trends; drop industries that violate pre-trend equality.

T2. Asian Financial Crisis (1997-98) & exchange-rate shock  
   – Imported-input prices spiked independent of tariffs.  
   – Mitigation: interact a post-1997 dummy with importer status; include industry-specific real exchange-rate exposure controls; re-estimate excluding 1997-1999.

T3. Endogenous switch into importing after tariff cuts  
   – Mitigation: define “importer” based on the pre-period only (“always importer” vs “never importer”); show robustness using inverse-probability weights based on predicted importing propensity in 1991–94.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)          # fast high-dim FE estimators
library(plm)             # for alternative checks
library(bacondecomp)     # pre-trend diagnostics

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# -------------------------------------------------
si  <- read_csv("indonesia_SI_1991_2001.csv")          # plant-level survey
tar <- read_csv("tariff_ISIC5_1991_2001.csv")          # input & output tariffs

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & basic cleaning
# -------------------------------------------------
df <- si %>%
      mutate(year = as.integer(year),
             isic5 = as.character(isic5)) %>%
      left_join(tar, by = c("isic5","year"))

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Construct key variables
# -------------------------------------------------
# 3.1 TFP (assume provided; else compute LP/OP separately)
#      Here: logtfp already in dataset
df <- df %>%
      group_by(plant_id) %>%
      mutate(importer_pre = as.numeric(mean(import_share[year<=1994], na.rm=TRUE) > 0)) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      mutate(post = if_else(year >= 1995, 1, 0),
             input_tariff  = input_tariff/100,      # put into 0-1 range
             output_tariff = output_tariff/100,
             Δinput_tariff = input_tariff - lag(input_tariff),
             Δoutput_tariff = output_tariff - lag(output_tariff))

# Keep balanced plants if desired
df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(logtfp), !is.na(input_tariff))

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main DID specification
# -------------------------------------------------
# Equation:
# logTFP_ijt = α_i + γ_t + β1*InputTariff_jt + β2*OutputTariff_jt
#            + β3*InputTariff_jt*ImporterPre_i + ε_ijt

did_main <- feols(logtfp ~ input_tariff + output_tariff +
                  input_tariff:importer_pre |
                  plant_id + year, data = df,
                  weights = ~ employment)          # optional weights

summary(did_main)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Event-study / dynamic effects (robustness)
# -------------------------------------------------
# Bin tariff changes into terciles
df <- df %>% group_by(isic5) %>%
             mutate(base_tariff = first(output_tariff[year==1991])) %>%
             ungroup() %>%
             mutate(high_cut = ntile(-base_tariff, 3)==1)  # highest initial tariffs

# Event-study with leads/lags of post*high_cut
event <- feols(logtfp ~ sunab(high_cut, year) |
               plant_id + year, data = df)

iplot(event)   # pre-trend visual check

# -------------------------------------------------
# 6. Endogeneity of importing check
# -------------------------------------------------
# Restrict to firms with stable importer status 1991-2001
stable <- df %>% group_by(plant_id) %>%
                 filter(n_distinct(importer_pre)==1) %>% ungroup()

did_stable <- feols(logtfp ~ input_tariff + output_tariff +
                    input_tariff:importer_pre |
                    plant_id + year, data = stable)

summary(did_stable)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts:

1. Input-tariff reductions lower the cost of imported intermediates ⇒ raise TFP, especially for firms already using imported inputs.  
2. Output-tariff reductions intensify competition, forcing inefficient plants to improve or exit; surviving firms’ average productivity should increase, but the mechanism is weaker and may take longer.

Back-of-the-envelope prior:  
•  A 10-percentage-point cut in input tariffs ⇒ ≈ 2–3 % increase in TFP for importers, ≈ 0.5–1 % for non-importers.  
•  A 10-percentage-point cut in output tariffs ⇒ ≈ 1 % increase in TFP on average.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
-------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually & statistically satisfied …… 0.8  
C2. Exogeneity of tariff shocks given WTO rules ………………… 0.9  
C3. No compositional changes (entry/exit bias) …………………… 0.6  
C4. No spillovers or interference across industries ……………… 0.8  
C5. Accurate measurement of tariffs & importer status ………… 0.7  

Average score ≈ 0.8 → credible but still dependent on pre-trend evidence and robustness to crisis years.

-------------------------------------------------
This plan outlines how to causally estimate and compare the productivity effects of reducing input vs. output tariffs, leveraging Indonesia’s staggered yet exogenous tariff liberalisation and rich plant-level panel data.
